analysis: Gilgit ǰáro keeps root prominence before the gender vowel, compatible both with old jára and the extended-adjective rule. input: jātá; explicitly paired with jā́yatē in the modern dictionary's full etymology

analysis: Palula ǰhóona/Biori ǰhúune and Strand ǰhʹôn- have early prominence on the lexical stem, with raising in the dialect comparison. analysis: Palula ǰhaamatroó and Gilgit jamac̣oó have late final oo; Guresi/Astori jamac̣óo have early final oo and Kohistani jamc̣ó is short. These are the same broad extended kinship formation with a genuine dialectal difference in mora alignment. Palula's oo raising implies an earlier early-accented final long vowel before its later advancement, as Liljegren's grammar explicitly proposes. Kalkoti ǰämäl ‘husband’s sister’ is not the same kin relation and requires separate etymological checking.
unresolved: The chronology of final-vowel advancement and the relation of the Kalkoti term remain open; no uniform Shinaic contour is justified.

input: jāmí and its old male/female-relative senses
analysis: Palula ẓamí and Sauji žamī́ preserve final prominence in an affinal kin term. Old root ā has shortened and the initial affricate has a regional retroflex/fricative outcome, while short versus long final i differs by source. analysis: Palula ǰóo/ǰúu is a raised early-accented citation with a present ǰáanu and perfective ǰóolu. analysis: Gilgit ǰaár has late long accent and the old friend/lover meaning, matching final-accent apocope. input: jihvā́, with an independent old juhū́ variant

analysis: Palula ǰhií~ ‘louse’ has late accent on old long ī, compatible with loss of final accented a. analysis: Palula ǰáandu is early-root-accented, and the old source already supplies barytone jī́vant as an alternative to final-accented jīvantá. Gilgit ǰoóno is late long, while ǰiino is unmarked. analysis: Gilgit ǰiil ‘life’ is long but unaccented in the primary headword, and older ǰil is short. The old entry has multiple suffixal quantities and accents, so the modern abstract noun needs formation selection before any prediction. Loss of v and contraction are plausible segmental steps.

input: jŕ̥mbhatē and independently attested jambháyati/jambh- formations

analysis: Palula tas/Biori tes is an oblique pronoun, with the old genitive tásya offering a closer input than the abstract stem tá. Both modern citations are short monosyllables and supply no mora contrast. Vowel quality and case-function redistribution are paradigm questions.

analysis: Strand tʹâc̣- and Gilgit tac̣- preserve the cutting/hewing root, with quantity differing across branches. analysis: Gilgit to, toó and -t are variants of a conditional/postverbal marker. analysis: Gilgit te ‘and’ is a short grammaticalized connective. analysis: Strand tʹâp- has early long root prominence, while an unmarked tâp- is also recorded. analysis: Astori tátto preserves a geminate stage that links old pt reduction to the other dialects. Kohistani táto/Guresi tátu are short, Gilgit taáto is late long, and Palula táatu is early long. analysis: Palula tapíǰa has accent on a derived inchoative stem before the citation ending; Gilgit tap- is a bare stem and older tapižóiki a suffixed infinitive. analysis: Gilgit c̣ak- ‘look/gaze’ is a reduced bound root, while the older infinitive carries a new ending. Guessing/thinking to inspecting is plausible, and the tr/ark-to-affricate history needs regional comparison. No marked modern root accent or matched finite cell is present.

analysis: Strand trakʹûli ‘spindle’ has early accent on the final root vowel before a feminine/derivational i.
